input.name: Walking to work
input.description: A small worldview about one everyday decision. It shows the things the format can express: foundations, jointly consumed premises, two independent arguments for the same conclusion, is/ought statements, and a mutually-justifying pair of statements (a cycle).

meta.author: example
meta.note: Nothing here is claimed to be true. It is a worked example of the format.

statements.text: Regular physical activity improves long-term health.
Walking for thirty minutes a day counts as regular physical activity.
I should act to protect my long-term health.
My commute takes about thirty minutes on foot.
Driving to work costs more than walking.
I should prefer the cheaper option when the options are otherwise equal.
It rains often where I live.
Walking in the rain without a raincoat is unpleasant.
I should own a good raincoat.
My assessments of my own habits are accurate.

meta.note: Part of a coherentist pair with habit-reports; neither is foundational.

statements.text: My reports about how I spend my time have matched outside observation.

arguments.justification: If protecting my health is something I should do, and walking my commute is a form of the activity that protects it, then walking my commute is something I should do.
Walking is the cheaper of two otherwise comparable ways to get to work, so the money principle selects it.

meta.note: An independent second argument for the same conclusion. The format never merges these.

arguments.justification: If I am going to walk regularly and it rains regularly, I will regularly be walking in the rain; a raincoat is what removes the unpleasantness of that.
A track record of accurate self-reports is evidence that my self-assessments are accurate.
It is my own assessment that my reports have matched observation, and my assessments of my habits are accurate.

meta.note: Together with reports-confirm-knowledge this is a cycle. The core allows it and reports it as an SCC.

arguments.justification: The thirty-minute figure comes from my own timing of the walk, which the track record says I can trust.
